prompt: What separates batch processing from stream processing, according to this lesson?
hint: Look at the input, not the clock.

choices.text: How fast each one can produce a result
choices.why: Speed follows from the difference; a five-minute batch job is still batch.

choices.text: Which programming language and which product is used to write each one
choices.why: Both shapes are written in Python in this lesson.

choices.text: How many machines the processing is spread over
choices.why: One machine runs both here; distribution is lesson 9’s subject.

choices.text: Whether the data it reads has an end
choices.why: Right: bounded data can be waited for, unbounded data cannot.

prompt: A job runs every five minutes and counts the rides that started in the previous five minutes. What is it?
hint: It waits for a piece to close, then reads all of it.

choices.text: A stream processor, because five minutes is close to real time
choices.why: Frequency does not make a stream; it still processes closed pieces.

choices.text: Neither, since a window that short is not a batch
choices.why: A batch can be any length, from a day to a few seconds.

choices.text: A batch job, run over short windows each of which has closed
choices.why: Right: bounded pieces, each processed once it is closed.

choices.text: A stream processor that has been configured to wait five minutes
choices.why: It reads nothing between runs; it is started on a schedule.

prompt: Which of these is unbounded data?
hint: Ask whether you could ever wait for all of it.

choices.text: The September rides export
choices.why: September ended; the export has a last row.

choices.text: A file uploaded by the maintenance team yesterday
choices.why: A file that has been uploaded is finished.

choices.text: The readings the dock sensors keep sending, day after day
choices.why: Right: they go on for as long as the company exists.

choices.text: The `docks.jsonl` file written by `sensors.py`
choices.why: The program stopped writing, so the file is bounded; the lesson reads it as if it were not.

prompt: Data that has an end, so that you can wait for all of it, is called ___ data.
hint: Batch processing works on it.

prompt: How many rides did the job run "as of" 01:00 on Tuesday count for Monday?
hint: The first run, before the backfill.

prompt: Why did the 01:00 job miss two of Monday’s rides?
hint: Compare when they happened with when they arrived.

choices.text: They had not reached the server when the job ran at 01:00
choices.why: Right: Passeio Público sent them at 07:02 on Tuesday.

choices.text: The job filtered on `arrived` instead of on `event_time` by mistake
choices.why: It filters the day on `event_time`; `asof` only limits what had arrived.

choices.text: The two rides started after midnight and belong to Tuesday instead
choices.why: They started on Monday morning, at 09:21 and 09:36.

choices.text: The CSV was appended to, not replaced
choices.why: Appending would add rides, not lose them; and it is replaced.

prompt: What is a backfill?
hint: It is about the past.

choices.text: Running a batch job again for windows already processed
choices.why: Right, for late data, a fixed bug or a new column.

choices.text: Filling the gaps in a table with values guessed from the rows around them
choices.why: That is imputation, a cleaning technique, and it invents data.

choices.text: Copying a database to a second machine so it has a backup
choices.why: That is a backup or a replica; nothing is recomputed.

choices.text: Sending a stream’s late events to a separate file
choices.why: That is one way of handling late data in a stream.

prompt: What made the backfill safe to run? Choose all that apply.
hint: Two things, both from lesson 3.

choices.text: The job replaces each day’s file instead of appending
choices.why: Yes: running it twice leaves one answer.

choices.text: The raw events were kept after the first run
choices.why: Yes: a backfill reads the past again.

choices.text: The job ran in under a second
choices.why: Speed makes it quick, not safe.

choices.text: The job was started by an orchestrator
choices.why: Here it was started by hand, and it was still safe.

prompt: Monday’s count is first published at 01:00 on Tuesday. What is the shortest honest description of that delay?
hint: Would a faster machine shorten it?

choices.text: It is caused by the job being slow, and a bigger machine would remove most of it
choices.why: The job takes moments; the wait is for the window to close.

choices.text: It is a mistake in the schedule that an orchestrator would correct
choices.why: The schedule is right: the job has to run after the day ends.

choices.text: It is caused by the late events from Passeio Público
choices.why: The delay exists on every night, outage or not.

choices.text: It is part of the design: the window has to close before it is counted
choices.why: Right: a day-long window ends at midnight, and the answer comes after.

prompt: After two runs of `consumer.py 300`, what number did `offset.txt` hold?
hint: The position of the next event to read.

prompt: A committed offset of 600 means what?
hint: Offsets start at 0.

choices.text: Event 600 was the last one processed
choices.why: The last one read was 599; 600 is where to start.

choices.text: The next event to read is at position 600
choices.why: Right: the offset written is where the next run starts.

choices.text: Events 0 to 599 were deleted
choices.why: Reading removes nothing from a log.

choices.text: 600 events are left to read
choices.why: There were 120 left: the log held 720.

prompt: How is reading a log different from taking messages off a queue?
hint: What happens to an event after it is read?

choices.text: The event stays, so another reader can read it too
choices.why: Right: each reader keeps its own offset.

choices.text: One consumer at a time can read a log
choices.why: The dock map and the van alert read the same log.

choices.text: Events in a log can be edited after reading
choices.why: A log is append-only: events are never changed.

choices.text: A log keeps events sorted by when they happened, a queue does not
choices.why: A log keeps the order of arrival, which this lesson shows is different.

prompt: The position a consumer has read up to, saved so a restart can continue, is its ___.
hint: A word Kafka uses too.

prompt: A bug in the consumer’s counting is fixed. How is a log-based consumer made to recount everything?
hint: Where does reading start?

choices.text: Ask the sensors to send every event again from the beginning
choices.why: The log already holds them; nobody has to send anything.

choices.text: Delete the log and let it fill up again with new events
choices.why: That throws away the past the recount needs.

choices.text: There is no way: a stream looks forward, not back
choices.why: Replaying from an old offset is what a log is good at.

choices.text: Set its offset back to 0 and let it read everything again
choices.why: Right: every event is read again by the fixed code.

prompt: Match each question to the clock it needs.
hint: Is it about the world or about the system?

pairs.left: how far behind the consumer is
when the last bicycle left Rua XV
how many events reached the server last minute

prompt: `lateness.py` found events that arrived after a later one but less than five seconds late. What explains them?
hint: Out of order is not the same as late.

choices.text: The Parque Barigui outage
choices.why: Those are more than a minute late.

choices.text: Two sensors whose readings crossed on the way
choices.why: Right: one to four seconds of delay is enough to swap two events.

choices.text: A bug in how `sensors.py` sorted the file
choices.why: The file is sorted by arrival on purpose, which is what a server sees.

choices.text: Sensors whose clocks drifted
choices.why: The generator gives every sensor a correct clock.

prompt: How many events did `lateness.py` find more than a minute late?
hint: Both outages together.

prompt: What cost does event time bring that processing time does not?
hint: An event from 08:20 can still be on its way.

choices.text: Waiting
choices.why: Right: the processor cannot know it has seen everything from 08:20.

choices.text: Every event has to be stored twice, once for each of the two clocks
choices.why: One event carries both fields in one line.

choices.text: It has to be converted to UTC before it can be compared
choices.why: Both clocks here are Curitiba’s and compare fine.

choices.text: A sensor cannot write a timestamp of its own
choices.why: It does: that is where event time comes from.

prompt: A dock sensor’s clock runs four minutes fast. What happens to its events downstream?
hint: Event time is only as good as the clock that wrote it.

choices.text: The watermark detects the drift and corrects each timestamp
choices.why: A watermark estimates progress; it does not know any clock is wrong.

choices.text: They are counted by processing time instead, automatically
choices.why: Nothing switches clocks for you.

choices.text: They land in the wrong windows, and nothing says so
choices.why: Right: a wrong stamp is used with complete confidence.

choices.text: They are dropped as late data by every window
choices.why: Running fast makes them look early, not late.

prompt: Match each window to what it is.
hint: Overlap, no overlap, or no fixed length.

pairs.right: closed by a gap with no events

prompt: Counted by arrival time, how many more rides did the 08:45 window hold than counted by event time?
hint: Compare the two columns of `windows.py`.

prompt: Both columns of `windows.py` total 64. Why is the arrival-time column still wrong?
hint: Where are the rides filed?

choices.text: It puts rides in the wrong quarter of an hour
choices.why: Right: the error is in which window, not in how many.

choices.text: It counts some rides twice and leaves out others, which balances by chance
choices.why: Each ride is counted once in each column.

choices.text: It is not wrong: when the totals agree, the columns agree
choices.why: 08:30 and 08:45 differ between the columns.

choices.text: It counts docks as well as undocks
choices.why: Both columns skip everything but undocks.

prompt: Rides are counted in 30-minute windows that start every 15 minutes. Why do the counts not add up to the day’s total?
hint: In how many windows is one ride?

choices.text: Sliding windows drop the events that fall on a boundary
choices.why: Nothing is dropped; events are shared.

choices.text: The windows are sessions, so they vary in length
choices.why: These have a fixed length and a fixed step.

choices.text: Each ride falls inside two of the overlapping windows
choices.why: Right: overlapping windows count each event once per window.

choices.text: Late rides are left out of the sliding windows
choices.why: Lateness is a separate question from the window’s shape.

prompt: Marta wants to know how long customers keep the app open in one go. Which window fits?
hint: The length is what is being measured.

choices.text: Tumbling windows of ten minutes, one after another
choices.why: A fixed length cuts one use of the app into pieces.

choices.text: A session window, one per customer visit
choices.why: Right: it follows the customer’s activity and ends after a quiet gap.

choices.text: A sliding window of an hour, updated every five minutes
choices.why: It counts recent activity, not one use from start to end.

choices.text: A single window covering the whole day
choices.why: That merges every visit of the day into one.

prompt: With an allowed lateness of two minutes, how many rides did `watermark.py` drop?
hint: Count the ids in the last line.

prompt: What does a watermark say?
hint: It is the processor’s estimate.

choices.text: That every event was delivered exactly once
choices.why: That is a delivery guarantee, a different question.

choices.text: That a window’s answer is final
choices.why: It is a bet; a late event can still prove it wrong.

choices.text: The arrival time of the latest event
choices.why: It is built from event time, not arrival.

choices.text: That no events older than it are expected any more
choices.why: Right: windows ending before it are sent.

prompt: Raising the allowed lateness from two to twenty-five minutes stopped the drops. What did it cost?
hint: Look at the times the windows were sent.

choices.text: Some rides were counted twice in the 08:15 window
choices.why: The counts match the event-time column exactly.

choices.text: More memory, because every event of the morning had to be held
choices.why: It holds four counters either way.

choices.text: Only the mornings with an outage were slower
choices.why: Every window waits, outage or not.

choices.text: Each count was sent well after its window had closed
choices.why: Right: the 08:00 window went out at 08:40 instead of 08:17.

prompt: Which allowed lateness would have caught Passeio Público’s rides in a stream?
hint: They arrived the next morning.

choices.text: Two minutes, if the processor had restarted
choices.why: A restart changes nothing about how late they were.

choices.text: Twenty-five minutes, as in the second run of `watermark.py`
choices.why: That caught Parque Barigui’s, which were half an hour late at most.

choices.text: A day or more: they came back the next morning
choices.why: Right: they were over twenty-one hours late.

choices.text: An hour, which is what streaming systems use by default
choices.why: There is no such default, and an hour is too short.

prompt: Which of these are ways to handle an event that arrives for a window already sent? Choose all that apply.
hint: Three were listed.

choices.text: Send a corrected count for the window
choices.why: Yes, when the reader can take a correction.

choices.text: Write it somewhere of its own
choices.why: Yes: then somebody can see how many there were.

choices.text: Let the nightly batch job count it
choices.why: Yes: the batch reads a closed day from raw events.

choices.text: Change its event time to the current window
choices.why: That files a ride under a time it did not happen.

prompt: Match each order of the two steps to what a crash between them causes.
hint: The step done first is the one that survives.

pairs.left: commit the offset, then do the work
do the work, then commit the offset
write the work and the offset together

prompt: After the crash, `consumer.py` ended with 515 rides on mornings that had 360. How many rides were counted twice?
hint: The batch from offset 300 to 599.

prompt: `consumer.py` writes its result and then commits its offset. Which guarantee does it give?
hint: What does a crash between the two cause?

choices.text: At most once, because the offset is committed in the end
choices.why: At most once commits first; this commits last.

choices.text: Exactly once, since the program never loses an event
choices.why: Never losing one is half; it repeats them.

choices.text: At least once, because a crash between the two repeats a batch
choices.why: Right: nothing is lost, and some events are counted twice.

choices.text: Effectively once, since the work is written first
choices.why: Its count went to 515: the repeat was not harmless.

prompt: Why did the same crash leave `keyed.py` at the right count?
hint: What is written for each ride?

choices.text: It commits its offset before writing its result, unlike `consumer.py`
choices.why: The order is the same; the batch was still delivered twice.

choices.text: A ride delivered twice is written to the same key twice
choices.why: Right: the write is idempotent.

choices.text: Its `--crash` flag stops the program at a different point
choices.why: It stops between the same two writes.

choices.text: It reads the log in smaller batches of events
choices.why: Both read 300 at a time.

prompt: Why can no network promise exactly-once delivery?
hint: Think of a sender that hears nothing back.

choices.text: Networks are too slow for the receiver to confirm each message in time
choices.why: Speed is not the problem; silence is.

choices.text: Every protocol duplicates its messages on purpose, as a safety measure
choices.why: Duplicates come from resending after silence, not from design.

choices.text: Messages arrive out of order on the way
choices.why: Order is a separate question from how many times.

choices.text: A lost message and a lost reply look the same
choices.why: Right: so the sender must resend or risk a loss.

prompt: Put the steps of the crash in `consumer.py` in order.
hint: The offset is the last thing written.
items: crash before the offset is committed
count offsets 300 to 599 a second time
trap: The count was written before the crash and the offset was not.

prompt: What is the main cost of the Lambda architecture?
hint: Count the paths.

choices.text: The same logic is written, run and kept up twice
choices.why: Right, and the two can disagree.

choices.text: The log must keep every event for years
choices.why: That is Kappa’s cost.

choices.text: It cannot produce an answer until the nightly batch job has run
choices.why: The speed layer answers during the day.

choices.text: Late events are lost for good
choices.why: The batch layer recomputes with them included.

prompt: In the Kappa architecture, how is a change to the logic applied to past data?
hint: There is no batch path.

choices.text: A nightly batch job recomputes the history
choices.why: That is Lambda’s batch layer.

choices.text: The new version replays the log from offset 0
choices.why: Right, into a new output that readers then switch to.

choices.text: It is not: Kappa only processes new events
choices.why: Replaying the past is the whole idea.

choices.text: The speed and serving layers are rebuilt
choices.why: Kappa has no layers of that kind.

prompt: Roda Livre’s log keeps events for seven days. Which architecture does that rule out for a change affecting last year?
hint: Which one depends on replaying the log?

choices.text: Lambda, since its speed layer reads the same log
choices.why: Lambda reprocesses from the batch layer’s raw copy.

choices.text: Neither, because a log can always be replayed
choices.why: Only what it still holds can be replayed.

choices.text: Both of them, because both depend on a log
choices.why: Lambda’s batch layer keeps all raw events.

choices.text: Kappa
choices.why: Right: last year is no longer in the log.

prompt: Which Roda Livre question earns a stream?
hint: What is done with the answer, and how soon?

choices.text: Rides per station last week, for planning next week’s van routes
choices.why: A day-old answer is fine for next week’s plan.

choices.text: Revenue per month, for the finance report
choices.why: Nobody acts on it within minutes.

choices.text: Which stations will be empty in the next half hour, for the van
choices.why: Right: the van has to move before it happens.

choices.text: Today’s rides so far, shown on the office screen
choices.why: Looked at, not acted on: hourly batch is enough.

prompt: A manager asks for the office dashboard "in real time". What does the section suggest asking first?
hint: The test is about action.

choices.text: Which streaming product the company already pays for
choices.why: The tool comes after the need.

choices.text: What decision it feeds, and how long that waits
choices.why: Right: "fresher than now" fits an hourly job.

choices.text: How many events a second the data source can produce
choices.why: Volume matters later; the need comes first.

choices.text: Whether the team prefers Lambda or Kappa
choices.why: That assumes a stream is needed at all.

prompt: Which of these does a stream make a team pay for that an hourly batch job does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: Everything this lesson showed.

choices.text: A process that never stops and must be watched
choices.why: Yes: somebody is woken when it stops.

choices.text: A watermark somebody has to choose
choices.why: Yes: and a decision about late data.

choices.text: State that must survive a crash
choices.why: Yes: plus duplicates to make harmless.

choices.text: Storing the raw events
choices.why: Batch needs them kept too, for backfills.

prompt: Put the steps of a stream window’s life in order.
hint: The watermark moves before the window is sent.
items: an event arrives with its event time
it is added to the window it belongs to
the watermark moves past the window’s end
a late event for it is dropped

prompt: A payment provider retries a webhook when it hears nothing back, and Roda Livre adds each payment to the day’s revenue. What is the first fix?
hint: The delivery is at least once.

choices.text: Record each payment under its own id, so a retry overwrites it
choices.why: Right: a retry writes the same key and changes nothing.

choices.text: Ask the provider to stop retrying
choices.why: Then a lost webhook is a payment nobody records.

choices.text: Add a watermark of one hour to the revenue
choices.why: Lateness is about time, not about repeats.

choices.text: Move the revenue report to a nightly batch job
choices.why: A batch would add the duplicates too.

prompt: A team counts rides per quarter of an hour by arrival time, and the chart shows a surge at 08:45 on Monday. What should they check first?
hint: Which clock files the rides?

choices.text: Whether more bicycles were put into service that morning
choices.why: That is the story the chart tells, and it may be false.

choices.text: Whether the daily total for Monday is lower than usual
choices.why: The total is the same by either clock.

choices.text: Whether a burst of old events arrived around 08:45
choices.why: Right: a burst of old events lands in the window it arrives in.

choices.text: Whether the consumer committed its offset correctly
choices.why: A repeat would raise many windows, not move rides between them.

prompt: A write that leaves the same result whether it is done once or twice is ___.
